mots.sens: This word means 'new' in the sense of something that is renewed or transformed. It is often used to describe a novelty that has a superior quality to the old, implying a break with the past. In the context of this verse, it emphasizes the promise of a renewed creation, where sin and suffering have no place, thus offering a profound eschatological hope.

The term 'earth' refers not only to the physical soil but also to the notion of the inhabited world. In the Bible, the earth is often associated with God's creation, the promise made to His people, and the manifestation of His glory. Here, the mention of a new earth evokes a complete restoration of divine order, where God dwells with His people in perfect communion.

The word 'sea' is often symbolic in the Scriptures, representing chaos, evil, and forces opposed to God. In this verse, the absence of the sea signifies the end of all that is in disorder and rebellion against God. This announces a state of eternal peace and security, where believers will no longer face the turmoil of this world.

1.epoque: This passage was written at the end of the 1st century, in a context of persecution of Christians and anticipation of divine deliverance. The Apostle John, exiled on the island of Patmos, receives revealing visions about the future of the Church and the world.
1.passage: In Revelation 21, John describes the vision of the new Jerusalem and the renewed creation. This chapter concludes the book of Revelation, offering a perspective of hope and ultimate redemption for believers.
1.culture: At that time, believers faced spiritual and material challenges. The promise of a new heaven and a new earth was a source of comfort, symbolizing God's victory over evil and the establishment of His eternal kingdom.
1.interpretation: This verse emphasizes the radical transformation that God will bring to His creation. The disappearance of the old heaven and the old earth symbolizes the end of suffering and injustices, while the promise of a new creation offers a living hope for believers in Christ.
1.commentaire: Revelation 21:1 reminds us that God is at work to restore all things. As Christians, we are called to live in anticipation of this promise, witnessing to the hope and peace that only Christ can bring. This vision encourages us not to cling to the transient things of this world, but to seek the eternal realities of God's kingdom.

mots.sens: This term means 'holy city' and evokes a city consecrated to God. In the biblical context, holiness is associated with purity, separation from sin, and divine presence. The new Jerusalem thus represents the fullness of communion between God and His people, an eschatological reality where believers will live in harmony with their Creator.

The 'new Jerusalem' symbolizes a complete restoration and redemption, in contrast to the earthly Jerusalem. This term emphasizes the idea of renewal and hope for believers, promising an eternal existence in glory. Theologically, this refers to God's promise to restore all things and create a place where there is no more suffering or sin.

This word means 'prepared' and evokes the idea of careful and intentional preparation. In the context of the bride adorning herself for her husband, it underscores the importance of purity and commitment in the relationship between God and His people. Spiritually, it reminds us that God has prepared a place of perfect communion for those who are faithful to Him.

The term 'bridegroom' refers to one who is engaged in a covenant relationship. In the Bible, this metaphor is often used to describe the relationship between Christ and the Church. It highlights the intimacy and love that God has for His people, as well as the call to faithfulness and spiritual preparation for believers.

2.epoque: This passage was written at the end of the 1st century, in a context where Christians faced persecution and spiritual challenges. The Apostle John, exiled on the island of Patmos, receives revelations about the end times and eschatological hope.
2.passage: Revelation 21 describes the vision of the new creation, where God establishes His dwelling among men. This chapter is part of the conclusion of the book, where God's promises are fully realized and the final victory over evil is proclaimed.
2.culture: In Jewish culture, the city of Jerusalem held deep significance, being the center of spiritual and religious life. The metaphor of the bride underscores the importance of covenants and commitments in marriage, reflecting God's love and faithfulness towards His people.
2.interpretation: The new Jerusalem represents the fulfillment of God's promises for His people, a place of peace and eternal communion. It reminds believers of their identity in Christ and their call to live in holiness, awaiting the return of their heavenly Bridegroom.
2.commentaire: This verse encourages us to live in anticipation of the realization of God's promises. As Christians, we are called to prepare spiritually for the meeting with our Bridegroom, cultivating an intimate relationship with Him. The vision of the new Jerusalem reminds us that our hope rests on God's faithfulness and the beauty of His grace, urging us to share this hope with the world around us.

mots.sens: This term refers to the sanctuary or temple, particularly the most sacred part where God's presence resides. In the context of this verse, it emphasizes the idea of intimate communion between God and humanity, where the tabernacle represents the divine presence among men. This evokes the restoration of the original relationship between God and humanity, a central theme in biblical theology.

This word means 'people' and is often used to designate the people of God. It evokes a community united by faith and relationship with God. In this verse, it emphasizes the idea that those who believe in God are called to be His people, thus reinforcing the collective identity of believers as a spiritual family.

This term means 'tabernacle' or 'dwelling,' and refers to a place where God resides among men. It recalls the tabernacle in the desert, a symbol of God's presence in the midst of His people. In this verse, it promises an eternal communion where God dwells among His people, reinforcing the idea of divine closeness and intimacy.

3.epoque: The book of Revelation was written at the end of the 1st century, in a context of persecution of Christians and spiritual crisis. Believers were seeking assurances about God's final victory over evil.
3.passage: This passage is found in the final chapter of Revelation, where John describes the new Jerusalem and the restoration of all things. It announces God's promise to live with His people in a new creation, without suffering or death.
3.culture: In Jewish culture, the tabernacle was the meeting place between God and His people. The idea of a God who dwells among men was deeply rooted in Israelite identity, and the verse reaffirms this promise in an eschatological context.
3.interpretation: This verse announces a future reality where God will be fully present with His people, marking the end of the separation caused by sin. It underscores the Christian hope of eternal communion with God, where believers will live in His presence without hindrance.
3.commentaire: This passage reminds us that our ultimate hope lies in God's presence among us. As believers, we are called to live in this reality now, cultivating an intimate relationship with God. This encourages us to share this good news with those who do not yet know the promise of His presence.

mots.sens: This word means 'death' and evokes not only the cessation of physical life but also the spiritual separation from God. In the biblical context, death is often seen as the ultimate enemy, a result of sin. The promise of the absence of death in this verse emphasizes Christ's victory over sin and death, bringing the hope of eternal life for believers.

This term refers to 'mourning' or 'sorrow,' and it is often associated with the emotional suffering caused by loss. In Jewish culture, mourning was a public and communal process, illustrating the profound impact of loss on human life. The absence of mourning in this verse indicates a state of perfect joy in the presence of God, where the sufferings of this life will no longer be present.

This word translates to 'cry' or 'lamentation,' and it evokes intense weeping and cries of pain. It is often used in Scripture to describe moments of great distress. The promise that these cries will no longer be heard underscores the complete restoration and eternal peace that God will bring to His people.

This term means 'pain' or 'suffering,' and it refers to physical or emotional suffering. In the context of this verse, the absence of pain means that all forms of suffering will be abolished in the kingdom of God. This reinforces the idea of a new creation where suffering has no place, thus offering profound comfort to believers.

4.epoque: The book of Revelation was written at the end of the first century, during a time when Christians faced persecution and severe trials. This historical context highlights the importance of hope and the promise of divine restoration.
4.passage: This verse is found in chapter 21, which describes the new Jerusalem and the promise of a glorious future for God's people. It marks the transition between judgment and redemption, emphasizing God's final victory over evil.
4.culture: In Jewish and Christian culture, the promise of eternal life and restoration is central. The concept of an existence without suffering and death resonates deeply with the eschatological expectations of believers, offering tangible hope in the face of life's struggles.
4.interpretation: This verse reminds us that God is a comforter who wipes away our tears and brings peace. The promise of an existence without suffering underscores God's benevolent nature and His desire to restore all things, offering us a perspective of hope for the future.
4.commentaire: As we meditate on this verse, we are encouraged to place our trust in God, who has promised to deliver us from all our sufferings. This compels us to live with the hope of eternal life, sharing this promise with those who suffer around us. The certainty that God will wipe away our tears drives us to live in joy, even amidst present trials.

mots.sens: This word means 'new' in the sense of something that is renewed or transformed. It is distinct from 'νεος' (neos), which simply means 'young.' In this context, 'kainos' evokes a radically new creation, indicating that God will restore all things in a way that surpasses our current understanding. This underscores the Christian hope for a new creation where sin and suffering will no longer exist.

This term means 'certain' or 'firm.' It expresses an unwavering assurance, indicating that God's promises are reliable and trustworthy. In this verse, it emphasizes that the words spoken by the one who sits on the throne are not merely promises but certainties that must be written and proclaimed, thereby strengthening the faith of believers.

This word means 'throne,' symbolizing authority and reign. In the biblical context, God's throne represents His sovereign power and ability to establish justice and peace. The mention of the throne in this verse reminds believers that God is in control of history and has the power to make all things new, thus offering great hope.

5.epoque: The book of Revelation was written at the end of the first century, in a context of persecution of Christians under the Roman Empire, which raised questions about the future and divine justice.
5.passage: This passage is located at the end of the book of Revelation, where John describes the vision of the new Jerusalem and God's promises for the future. It is a message of hope and redemption for believers, affirming that God will restore all things.
5.culture: In Jewish and Christian culture, the idea of 'newness' is deeply linked to the promise of redemption and renewal. Believers awaited a Messiah who would bring a new beginning and a new order.
5.interpretation: This verse highlights God's sovereignty over all creation and His promise of renewal. It reminds believers that despite present trials, God has a plan to restore and make all things new, which is a source of comfort and hope.
5.commentaire: This passage calls us to live in anticipation of the new creation that God promises. As Christians, we are called to share this hope with the world, testifying to God's faithfulness and living in a way that reflects this newness in our daily lives. The certainty of God's promises should encourage us to persevere in faith, knowing that He is capable of transforming our lives and our world.

mots.sens: The word 'ἄλφα' (alpha) is the first letter of the Greek alphabet. In the biblical context, it symbolizes the beginning, the first cause of all things. By designating Himself as the Alpha, Christ affirms His primordial role in creation and history, underscoring that He is the origin of all that exists.

The word 'ὦμέγα' (omega) is the last letter of the Greek alphabet. It represents the end, the culmination of all things. By presenting Himself as the Omega, Jesus declares that He is also the one who concludes history, bringing meaning and purpose to creation, which is essential for understanding His divine authority.

The word 'πηγή' (pēgē) means 'source' or 'fountain.' In a spiritual sense, it evokes a source of eternal life and deep satisfaction. By offering this source of living water, Jesus presents Himself as the one who quenches humanity's spiritual thirst, thus highlighting His ability to give eternal life.

The word 'ζωής' (zōēs) means 'life.' In the biblical context, it refers to eternal life, the fullness of life in communion with God. This life is not only a physical existence but also a deep spiritual relationship with the Creator, which is central to the message of salvation offered by Christ.

6.epoque: This passage was written at the end of the first century, during a time of persecution of Christians and uncertainty for the Church. Believers faced major challenges, both spiritual and material.
6.passage: Chapter 21 of Revelation describes the new creation, where God establishes His eternal kingdom. This verse emphasizes Christ's sovereignty over history and the promise of eternal life for those who believe in Him.
6.culture: In Jewish and Christian culture, water is often symbolic of purification and life. The idea of a source of living water resonates deeply with messianic expectations and God's promise to restore His people.
6.interpretation: This verse reveals the eternal nature of Christ, the Alpha and the Omega, who encompasses all time and space. He offers all who thirst a promise of spiritual satisfaction, emphasizing that eternal life is a free gift for those who turn to Him.
6.commentaire: This passage reminds us that Jesus is both the beginning and the end of our faith. As believers, we are invited to come to Him to quench our spiritual thirst. It is essential to recognize that this eternal life is a free gift, and we must share this good news with those seeking meaning in their lives.

mots.sens: This verb means 'to conquer' or 'to overcome'. It is often used in the New Testament to describe spiritual victory over sin, the world, and Satan. In the context of this verse, it evokes the idea of perseverance and success in faith, emphasizing that those who triumph through their trust in Christ will receive eternal blessings. The theological significance of this word is profound, as it reminds us that victory is already secured in Christ for those who believe.

This term means 'heir' and refers to a person who receives an inheritance, often related to divine promises. In the biblical context, it evokes the idea of belonging to the family of God and the blessings that come with it. Spiritually, this underscores that believers, as heirs of God, share in Christ the promises of eternal life and communion with Him.

This word means 'God' and is central to understanding the divine nature. It represents the supreme authority, the creator, and the sovereign of the universe. In this verse, the affirmation 'I will be his God' emphasizes the intimate and personal relationship that God establishes with those who are faithful to Him, reinforcing the idea of closeness between the believer and the Creator.

This term means 'son' and evokes a relationship of filiation. In the biblical context, being called 'son of God' implies a spiritual identity and a privileged position in the divine family. It highlights the dignity and honor of those who believe, conferring upon them a status of heirs and beneficiaries of divine promises.

7.epoque: The book of Revelation was written at the end of the 1st century, in a context of persecution of Christians under the Roman Empire, where faith was being tested.
7.passage: This verse is found in chapter 21, which describes the new Jerusalem and God's promises for those who are faithful to Him, highlighting the contrast between present suffering and future glory.
7.culture: In Jewish and Christian culture, the idea of inheritance was very important, symbolizing not only material possessions but also spiritual blessings and an intimate relationship with God.
7.interpretation: This verse affirms that those who overcome by faith will inherit God's promises, establishing a father-son relationship with Him. It emphasizes the importance of perseverance in faith to receive eternal blessings.
7.commentaire: This passage encourages us to persevere in our faith despite trials, reminding us that victory is promised to those who remain faithful. As heirs of God, we are called to live in the light of this promise, cultivating our relationship with Him and sharing this hope with those around us.

mots.sens: This term means 'cowardly' or 'timid', and it evokes an excessive fear that prevents acting according to faith. In the spiritual context, it refers to those who, out of fear, renounce their commitment to God. Cowardice is condemned here as it hinders living fully the truth of the Gospel.

This word means 'unbelieving' or 'non-believer'. It designates those who reject faith in Christ and His promises. Unbelief is an attitude that distances one from God's grace and leads to eternal consequences, highlighting the importance of believing to receive eternal life.

This term refers to 'fornicator' or 'adulterer'. It encompasses all forms of sexual immorality, which are often symbolic of spiritual unfaithfulness to God. Theologically, this represents a separation from divine holiness and a rejection of the moral standards established by God.

This word means 'liar' and designates those who deceive or distort the truth. Deception is an affront to the nature of God, who is Truth. In the context of this verse, liars are warned of the seriousness of their sin, as truth is essential for communion with God.

8.epoque: The book of Revelation was written at the end of the 1st century, in a context of persecution of Christians by the Roman Empire. Believers faced major challenges to remain faithful to their faith in a hostile world.
8.passage: This passage is located at the end of Revelation, where John describes the new Jerusalem and the final judgment. It highlights the contrast between the destinies of the righteous and the unrighteous, emphasizing the seriousness of the consequences of sin.
8.culture: In the culture of the time, idolatry and immorality were common, often encouraged by society. Christians were called to stand out through their conduct and faithfulness to God, despite cultural pressures.
8.interpretation: This verse warns against the eternal consequences of sin and unbelief. It reminds us that those who persist in these behaviors without repentance will be excluded from the presence of God, underscoring the importance of living a life in accordance with Christ's teachings.
8.commentaire: This passage invites us to reflect on our own lives and our commitment to God. It is essential not to let fear or unbelief divert us from our faith. As believers, we are called to live in truth and holiness, relying on God's grace to overcome our weaknesses.

mots.sens: The word 'νύμφη' designates a bride or fiancée. In the biblical context, it evokes the idea of an intimate and sacred relationship between Christ and the Church, often symbolized by marriage. The root of this word emphasizes commitment and unconditional love, which is central in Christian theology regarding the relationship between the believer and the Savior.

The term 'Ἀρνίον' means 'lamb' and refers to Jesus Christ, the Lamb of God, who was sacrificed for the sin of humanity. This word evokes gentleness, innocence, and sacrifice, thus highlighting Christ's redemptive role. In this verse, it recalls the connection between Christ's sacrifice and the establishment of His Church, His bride.

The word 'ἄγγελος' means 'messenger' and is often used to designate spiritual beings sent by God. In this verse, the angel plays a crucial role in revealing divine truths to John. This underscores the importance of divine revelation and the ministry of angels in fulfilling God's plan for humanity.

9.epoque: The book of Revelation was written at the end of the 1st century, at a time when the Christian Church faced persecution and internal challenges. This historical context underscores the importance of hope and Christ's final victory over evil.
9.passage: This passage is found in a section of Revelation where John receives visions of the end times and the new creation. It introduces the vision of the New Jerusalem and the bride, symbolizing the Church, which will be united with Christ in an eternal relationship.
9.culture: In Jewish culture, marriage was a powerful symbol of the covenant between God and His people. The image of the bride in this verse evokes themes of faithfulness, love, and promise, which were deeply rooted in biblical tradition.
9.interpretation: The bride, the wife of the Lamb, represents the Church, which is called to be pure and faithful to her Husband, Jesus Christ. This passage highlights the beauty and glory of the relationship between Christ and believers, who are called to live in communion with Him in anticipation of His return.
9.commentaire: This verse reminds us that the Church is precious in God's sight and is destined for an eternal union with Christ. As believers, we are called to live in this reality, cultivating our relationship with the Lord and remaining faithful to His call. This encourages us to prepare for the day when we will be united with Him in glory.

mots.sens: The word 'πόλις' means 'city' and evokes an organized community, often with implications of security and prosperity. In the context of this verse, it refers to the 'holy city, Jerusalem,' symbolizing God's presence among His people. Theologically, this emphasizes the idea of redemption and the ultimate restoration of humanity in perfect communion with God.

The term 'δόξα' translates to 'glory' and refers to divine splendor and majesty. In this verse, the glory of God is a central element, illustrating the perfection and beauty of the new Jerusalem. Spiritually, this reminds believers that the glory of God is the source of our hope and eternal future.

The verb 'καταβαίνω' means 'to descend' and implies a movement from above to below. In this passage, it describes the descent of the holy city from heaven, symbolizing divine intervention in human history. This underscores the idea that God does not remain distant but actively engages with His people.

The word 'πνεῦμα' means 'spirit' and evokes the living and dynamic presence of God. In this context, the fact that John is transported 'in spirit' emphasizes the importance of divine revelation and spiritual experience. This reminds believers that understanding spiritual truths requires sensitivity to the work of the Holy Spirit.

10.epoque: This passage was written at the end of the 1st century, during a time when Christians faced persecution and uncertainty, seeking encouragement in the promise of a new creation.
10.passage: In chapter 21 of Revelation, John describes the vision of the new Jerusalem, symbolizing the fulfillment of God's promises and the final restoration of all things. This passage highlights the contrast between the current world and the future reality that God is preparing for His people.
10.culture: At that time, Jerusalem was perceived as the spiritual center of the Jewish world. The vision of the new Jerusalem represents a radical transformation, where God's presence is fully accessible to all believers, transcending cultural and geographical limitations.
10.interpretation: This verse reveals the promise of eternal communion between God and His people, where divine glory is manifest. The descent of the holy city symbolizes the fulfillment of God's promises and the establishment of an eternal kingdom, where suffering and separation are no more.
10.commentaire: This passage reminds us that our Christian hope rests on the promise of a future reality where God dwells among His people. As believers, we are called to live in anticipation of this new Jerusalem, cultivating an intimate relationship with God even now. We must also share this hope with those around us, witnessing to the glory of God in our lives.

mots.sens: The term 'iaspēs' refers to a precious stone, often associated with beauty and splendor. In antiquity, jasper was considered a symbol of purity and perfection. The mention of this stone here underscores the majesty and glory of the new Jerusalem, representing the divine presence. Spiritually, this evokes the beauty of communion with God and the brilliance of His eternal kingdom.

The word 'diaphanós' means 'transparent' or 'clear,' indicating a purity without blemish. In the biblical context, this transparency can symbolize the clarity of divine revelation and the absence of sin. It also emphasizes that in God's kingdom, everything is pure and without darkness, thus representing the light of Christ that illuminates all.

11.epoque: Revelation was written at the end of the 1st century, in a context of persecution of Christians under the Roman Empire, which influenced its message of hope and ultimate victory.
11.passage: This verse is situated in the description of the new Jerusalem, a symbol of the restoration and redemption promised to believers. Chapter 21 speaks of the end of suffering and the establishment of a new order where God dwells among His people.
11.culture: In ancient culture, precious stones were often associated with royalty and divinity, representing wealth and splendor. The descriptions of the new Jerusalem use this language to communicate the greatness of God's kingdom.
11.interpretation: The brilliance of the new Jerusalem, resembling a precious stone, symbolizes the glory of God and the beauty of His kingdom. This reminds us that our inheritance in Christ is of inestimable value and that we are called to live in the light of this reality.
11.commentaire: This verse encourages us to contemplate the beauty and splendor of God's presence, which is promised to all who believe. As Christians, we must live in anticipation of this reality, reflecting the light of Christ in our daily lives. This compels us to seek purity and holiness, reminding us that our future is in Christ, in an eternal kingdom of joy and peace.

mots.sens: This term refers to a 'wall,' a structure of protection and separation. In the biblical context, the wall symbolizes the security and holiness of God's city, representing the divine presence that protects His people. The great wall of the New Jerusalem also evokes the idea of a separation between the holy and the profane, highlighting the purity and glory of the Eternal.

The word 'gates' refers to entrances, access points that allow entry into a sacred space. In biblical culture, gates are often symbols of welcome and judgment. The twelve gates of the New Jerusalem, guarded by angels, symbolize access to God's presence and divine protection, while also recalling the heritage of the twelve tribes of Israel.

This term means 'angels,' messengers of God. In the Bible, angels play a crucial role as protectors and servants of divine will. Their presence at the gates of the New Jerusalem underscores the importance of divine mediation and the spiritual protection offered to those who enter the holy city.

The word 'tribes' refers to the groups that make up the people of Israel, each having a distinct identity and heritage. In the context of the New Jerusalem, the names of the twelve tribes on the gates symbolize inclusion and the continuity of God's covenant with His people. It also reminds us that the Church, as the new people of God, is rooted in the history of Israel.

12.epoque: This passage was written at the end of the 1st century, in a context of persecution of Christians and reflection on the future of the Church in the face of opposition.
12.passage: Chapter 21 of Revelation describes the New Jerusalem, a symbol of the final restoration and perfect union between God and His people. This verse highlights the structure of the city and its connection to the promises made to Israel.
12.culture: In Jewish culture, city gates were places of gathering and decision. They also symbolized security and national identity, which is reinforced by the mention of the tribes of Israel.
12.interpretation: The mention of the twelve gates and angels reminds us that access to God's presence is divinely ordained and protected. It also emphasizes that the New Jerusalem is the place where God's promise to His people is fully realized, encompassing all who believe in Christ.
12.commentaire: This verse reminds us that God has prepared a place of security and communion for His people, a space where holiness and divine protection reign. As believers, we are called to enter into this relationship with God, recognizing our heritage in Christ and living in accordance with the values of His kingdom. The New Jerusalem is an encouragement for us to persevere in faith, knowing that our future is secure in Him.

mots.sens: This term refers to a gate or entrance, symbolizing both access and separation. In the biblical context, gates are often symbols of protection and passage to a sacred space. The presence of twelve gates in the New Jerusalem indicates God's openness to all nations, highlighting the universal scope of salvation.

This word means 'east' or 'rising sun', symbolizing a new beginning and hope. In Jewish culture, the east is often associated with divine light and revelation. By mentioning the east, the text evokes the glory of God manifesting in the New Jerusalem, bringing light and life to those who enter.

This term means 'west' or 'setting sun', often associated with the end of a cycle or death. In the context of the New Jerusalem, this can symbolize the end of suffering and darkness, marking the entrance into an eternity full of light and peace. It reminds us that, even though earthly life has its endings, God's promise is one of a radiant eternity.

13.epoque: The book of Revelation was written at the end of the 1st century, during a time of persecution for Christians, seeking to encourage them in their faith in the face of adversity.
13.passage: This verse is situated in the description of the New Jerusalem, a symbol of God's eternal presence among His people. Chapter 21 speaks of the final restoration and redemption, where God dwells with men.
13.culture: In Jewish culture, gates held great significance, often linked to places of gathering and judgment. The city gates were symbols of security and welcome, reinforcing the idea of the New Jerusalem as a place of welcome for all.
13.interpretation: The twelve gates, oriented toward each direction, symbolize the universality of the Gospel message and the invitation for all peoples to enter the kingdom of God. This emphasizes that access to God's presence is open to all, without distinction.
13.commentaire: This passage reminds us that God has prepared a place of welcome for His people, where everyone can enter and live in His presence. As Christians, we are called to share this good news and invite others to discover the light and hope found in Christ. The New Jerusalem is a symbol of unity and peace, encouraging us to live in harmony with our brothers and sisters in faith.

mots.sens: This word means 'foundation' and evokes the idea of a base or support upon which something is built. In the biblical context, it refers to the solidity and permanence of the Christian faith. The foundations of the city symbolize the stability and security of the New Jerusalem, anchored in divine revelation and the authority of the apostles.

This term refers to an 'apostle', literally meaning 'sent one'. The apostles were direct witnesses of Christ's resurrection and had the mission to spread the Gospel. Their names on the foundations of the city highlight the importance of their role in establishing the Church and their spiritual authority, rooted in the divine mission.

The word 'Lamb' refers to Jesus Christ, often called the Lamb of God. This evokes sacrifice and redemption, emphasizing that the foundation of the Christian faith rests on Christ's sacrifice. The mention of the Lamb in this verse reminds believers that their hope and salvation are centered on Him.

14.epoque: The book of Revelation was written at the end of the 1st century, in a context of persecution of Christians, as the Church sought to assert itself in the face of opposition and moral decay of the Roman era.
14.passage: This verse is situated in chapter 21, which describes the vision of the New Jerusalem, a symbol of final redemption and perfect union between God and His people. It emphasizes the importance of the apostles in the foundation of this heavenly reality.
14.culture: In Jewish culture, the foundations of a city were of great importance, representing security and permanence. The names of the apostles on the foundations of the New Jerusalem testify to the spiritual heritage and authority they left to the Church.
14.interpretation: This passage highlights the inseparable link between the Church and the apostles, emphasizing that the Christian faith is built on the teachings and testimony of those who were sent by Christ. The New Jerusalem, with its foundations, represents the community of believers, rooted in the truth of the Gospel.
14.commentaire: The mention of the twelve apostles on the foundations of the city reminds us that our faith rests on solid and historical truths. As believers, we are called to build our spiritual lives on these foundations, relying on the teachings of those who witnessed Christ's resurrection. This encourages us to live in accordance with the Gospel and to pass this truth on to future generations.

mots.sens: This word means 'measure' and comes from a root that evokes the idea of delimitation and precision. In the biblical context, it is often associated with the notion of divine justice and order. The measure here emphasizes the perfection and harmony of the New Jerusalem, symbolizing God's will to create a holy and perfect space for His people.

This term means 'gold' and is often used to symbolize value, purity, and divine glory. In biblical culture, gold is associated with spiritual wealth and the presence of God. The use of a golden reed to measure the city indicates that the New Jerusalem is of inestimable value and designed according to divine standards.

This word means 'city' and evokes not only a physical place but also a community of believers. In the New Testament, the notion of city carries an eschatological significance, representing the kingdom of God and the communion of saints. The mention of the city in this verse emphasizes the idea of a place of refuge and security for those who are in Christ.

This term means 'wall' and is often associated with protection and security. In the context of the New Jerusalem, the walls symbolize the separation between the holy and the profane, as well as the security offered by God to His people. It also evokes the strength and permanence of God's promise of protection.

15.epoque: This passage was written at the end of the 1st century, in a context of persecution of Christians, as the apostle John received visions about the future of the Church and the final judgment.
15.passage: Revelation 21 describes the New Jerusalem, a vision of final restoration and perfect communion between God and His people. This chapter highlights the beauty and perfection of the heavenly city, which will be the dwelling place of the redeemed.
15.culture: In Jewish culture, measurement was often used to express order and holiness. The city of Jerusalem held paramount importance, symbolizing God's presence among His people and the place of worship.
15.interpretation: The measurement of the city with a golden reed emphasizes the perfection and holiness of the New Jerusalem. This reminds believers that God has a precise and perfect plan for their future, where they will live in communion with Him in an environment of peace and security.
15.commentaire: This verse reminds us that God is a God of order and precision, and that His promise of the New Jerusalem is a reality to which we can aspire. As believers, we must live in anticipation of this promise, seeking to reflect God's holiness and glory in our daily lives. The vision of the New Jerusalem encourages us to persevere in faith, knowing that our future is assured in Christ.

mots.sens: This term means 'city' and evokes a place of gathering, community, and governance. In the context of Revelation, it represents not only a physical space but also a spiritual reality where God dwells among His people. The notion of 'city' here emphasizes the idea of perfect communion between God and humanity in the New Jerusalem.

The word 'stadion' refers to a unit of measurement, equivalent to about 185 meters. In this verse, the mention of twelve thousand stadia highlights the immensity and grandeur of the New Jerusalem, symbolizing the abundance of God's presence. Spiritually, this indicates the fullness of eternal life that God offers to His elect.

This term, meaning 'of the same measure', reinforces the idea of balance and harmony in the design of the city. The symmetry of length, width, and height evokes divine perfection and order in the kingdom of God. It reminds us that in eternal life, everything will be in perfect harmony under the sovereignty of Christ.

16.epoque: Revelation was written at the end of the first century, in a context of persecution of Christians, which strengthened the hope for future deliverance and divine restoration.
16.passage: This passage is situated in the vision of the New Jerusalem, which represents the culmination of God's plan for humanity, where He establishes His dwelling among men. Chapter 21 describes the end of suffering and the advent of an era of peace and communion with God.
16.culture: In Jewish and Roman culture, the city was a symbol of security, identity, and community. The description of the New Jerusalem as a perfect city resonates with the messianic expectations of God's people.
16.interpretation: The square shape of the city and its equal dimensions symbolize the balance and perfection of the kingdom of God. This emphasizes that in the presence of God, everything is in harmony and fullness, offering an image of eternal life without flaw.
16.commentaire: This verse reminds us that the New Jerusalem is a place prepared by God for His people, where peace and perfection reign. As believers, we are called to live in anticipation of this reality, cultivating our relationship with God here and now, in hope of this eternal communion.

mots.sens: This verb means 'to measure' and evokes the idea of determining precise dimensions. In the context of Revelation 21:17, it emphasizes the importance of divine measurement, which establishes standards and limits. The measurement here is not only physical but also symbolizes perfection and divine order in the New Jerusalem, indicating that everything conforms to God's will.

This term means 'walls' and refers to the protective structure of the New Jerusalem. The walls symbolize security and separation from evil, while also representing the glory of God. In the eschatological context, they testify to the solidity and permanence of God's presence among His people.

This word designates a unit of measurement, equivalent to about 45 centimeters. In this verse, it underscores divine precision in the construction of the New Jerusalem. The mention of 'measure of man' indicates that the dimensions are understandable and accessible to humans, while reflecting the greatness of God's work.

This term means 'angel' and designates a messenger of God. In the context of this verse, the angel is an intermediary who reveals the divine measurement. This underscores divine authority and communication between heaven and earth, reminding us that God uses spiritual beings to convey His will and revelations.

17.epoque: The book of Revelation was written at the end of the first century, in a context of persecution of Christians under the Roman Empire. Believers sought encouragement and assurance regarding their faith and the future promised by God.
17.passage: This verse is situated in a vision of the New Jerusalem, describing the beauty and perfection of the heavenly city. It is part of a larger passage that reveals the end of times and the restoration of all things under God's reign.
17.culture: In Jewish and Christian culture, measurement often has symbolic significance, representing divine order and perfection. The precise dimensions of the New Jerusalem also recall the descriptions of the construction of the temple in the Old Testament, emphasizing the continuity of God's work.
17.interpretation: The measurement of the wall, which is 144 cubits, symbolizes perfection and fullness of the new creation. It indicates that all that is divine is in harmony and conforms to God's will, offering an image of security and protection for God's people.
17.commentaire: This verse reminds us that God is a God of measurement and order, and that everything in His creation is perfect. As believers, we can find comfort and assurance in the promise of the New Jerusalem, where we will be secure in the presence of God. It also calls us to live in accordance with divine standards, recognizing that our lives should reflect the glory and holiness of our Creator.

mots.sens: The word 'iaspis' designates a precious stone, often associated with beauty and splendor. In antiquity, this stone was prized for its rich color and hardness. Spiritually, it symbolizes the perfection and glory of God, emphasizing that the New Jerusalem is a place of divine beauty where nothing unclean enters.

The term 'chrusos' means 'gold', a precious metal that represents wealth, purity, and eternal value. In the Bible, gold is often used to describe the glory of God and the value of heavenly things. Here, it emphasizes that the city is made of pure gold, illustrating the divine nature and perfection of the kingdom of God.

18.epoque: The book of Revelation was written at the end of the first century in a context of Christian persecution, where believers sought hope and the promise of Christ's victory over evil.
18.passage: This passage is situated in the description of the New Jerusalem, a symbol of God's eternal reign with His people, where the beauty and perfection of divine creation are revealed.
18.culture: In Jewish and Christian culture, precious stones and gold are often used to symbolize divine glory and spiritual wealth, reinforcing the idea that the kingdom of God is of unparalleled beauty.
18.interpretation: This verse illustrates the magnificence of the New Jerusalem, a place where the presence of God is manifested in all its splendor. The wall of jasper and the city of pure gold evoke a spiritual reality where beauty and purity are in harmony with the holiness of God.
18.commentaire: The description of the New Jerusalem reminds us that our hope in Christ is not limited to this life but extends to an eternal reality of glory. As believers, we are called to live in anticipation of this divine beauty, cultivating a life of purity and holiness, thus reflecting the light of Christ in an often dark world.

mots.sens: Jasper is a precious stone often associated with beauty and splendor. In antiquity, it was considered a symbol of protection and strength. Spiritually, jasper evokes the glory of God and the perfection of His kingdom, emphasizing the idea that heaven is a place of purity and magnificence.

Sapphire is a bluish precious stone, symbolizing wisdom and discernment. In the Scriptures, it is often linked to divine revelation and knowledge. Its inclusion among the foundations of the heavenly city underscores the importance of divine wisdom in eternal life.

Chalcedony is a translucent precious stone that represents peace and harmony. In the biblical context, it symbolizes unity and communion among believers. As a foundation of the New Jerusalem, it reminds us of the perfect harmony that will reign in the kingdom of God.

Emerald is a green precious stone, often associated with life and rebirth. It evokes the beauty of God's creation and the eternal life offered to believers. In this verse, it highlights the richness and vitality of the kingdom of God, where life abounds in fullness.

19.epoque: The Book of Revelation was written at the end of the first century, during a time of persecution for Christians, which provides a context of suffering and hope for the recipients of the message.
19.passage: This passage is found in chapter 21, which describes the New Jerusalem, a symbol of the fulfillment of God's promises. It highlights the beauty and splendor of the kingdom of God, contrasting with the trials of earthly life.
19.culture: In ancient culture, precious stones were often used to symbolize wealth, beauty, and status. Their presence in the context of the New Jerusalem underscores the grandeur and magnificence of the kingdom of God.
19.interpretation: The foundations adorned with precious stones illustrate the perfection and beauty of the kingdom of God. Each stone has a spiritual significance, representing aspects of the divine nature and eternal life. This reminds us that our inheritance in Christ is of immeasurable value.
19.commentaire: This verse invites us to contemplate the beauty of heaven and to remember that our faith is founded on solid divine promises. As believers, we must live in anticipation of this glorious reality, striving to reflect the splendor of God in our daily lives. The description of the foundations of the heavenly city encourages us to aspire to holiness and spiritual beauty.

mots.sens: The term 'sardios' refers to a precious stone, often associated with the color red. In the biblical context, it symbolizes strength and vitality, evoking the beauty and splendor of divine creation. Spiritually, it can represent the sacrifice of Christ, whose blood was shed for our redemption.

The 'chrysolite' is a golden-colored precious stone, representing wealth and glory. In biblical tradition, this stone can symbolize divine light and the presence of God. Theologically, it reminds us of the promise of the heavenly inheritance awaiting believers.

The 'amethyst' is a purple precious stone, often associated with wisdom and temperance. Its name means 'not drunk', which evokes clarity of mind and spiritual purity. In the context of the New Jerusalem, it symbolizes the peace and serenity that believers will find in Christ.

20.epoque: The Book of Revelation was written at the end of the first century, in a context of persecution of Christians under the Roman Empire, which influenced the apocalyptic style and imagery used by the author.
20.passage: This passage is found in chapter 21, which describes the New Jerusalem, the eternal dwelling place of believers. It emphasizes the beauty and glory of this heavenly city, built with precious materials.
20.culture: In ancient culture, precious stones were often associated with royalty and divinity, representing wealth and beauty. The apostles and early Christians used these symbols to illustrate the greatness of the divine promise.
20.interpretation: Each stone mentioned in this verse contributes to depicting the splendor of the New Jerusalem. They symbolize not only physical beauty but also the attributes of God and the spiritual inheritance of believers, who are called to live in this eternal glory.
20.commentaire: This verse reminds us that the New Jerusalem is a place of perfection and beauty, where every detail reflects the glory of God. As believers, we are called to aspire to this heavenly reality, to live in the light, and to testify to the splendor of our inheritance in Christ. This encourages us to persevere in our faith, knowing that our future is secured in the presence of God.

mots.sens: This word means 'gate' and is used to designate an entrance or opening in a wall. In the context of the New Jerusalem, the gates symbolize access to the presence of God. Each gate being a pearl evokes the beauty and spiritual value of access to eternal life.

This term refers to a 'pearl', symbolizing purity and wealth. In Jewish culture, pearls are often associated with wisdom and divine beauty. In this verse, the gates made of pearls illustrate the magnificence of the New Jerusalem and the importance of access to God.

This word means 'gold' and represents wealth, purity, and immeasurable value. In the context of the New Jerusalem, pure gold, like transparent glass, symbolizes the perfection and holiness of the heavenly environment. This underscores the divine nature and glory of the presence of God.

This term means 'city' and evokes a place of gathering and community. In the Book of Revelation, the city represents the community of redeemed believers and their eternal dwelling with God. This emphasizes the idea of divine communion and security in the presence of God.

21.epoque: Revelation was written at the end of the first century, in a context of Christian persecution and eschatological expectation, where believers hoped for deliverance and the restoration of all things through Christ.
21.passage: This passage is found at the end of the Book of Revelation, where John describes the vision of the New Jerusalem, a symbol of the fulfillment of God's promises and the restoration of communion between God and humanity.
21.culture: In ancient culture, pearls and gold were symbols of wealth and value, often associated with divinity and beauty. The description of the New Jerusalem uses these symbols to illustrate the magnificence of the presence of God.
21.interpretation: The twelve gates of pearls and the street of pure gold represent the beauty and grandeur of the kingdom of God. They also symbolize direct access to God, offering an image of security and perfection for those who are in Christ.
21.commentaire: This verse reminds us that God's promise for His children is eternal communion in a place of beauty and perfection. As believers, we are called to live in anticipation of this reality, preparing to enter into the presence of God with joy and gratitude. The magnificence of the New Jerusalem encourages us to seek the things above and to live according to the values of the kingdom of God here on earth.

mots.sens: This term refers to the sanctuary or temple, often used to designate the most sacred part of the temple, the Holy of Holies. In the context of this verse, it emphasizes the absence of a physical place of worship, indicating that the divine presence is not confined to a particular space. Theologically, this expresses God's closeness to His people, where His presence is accessible and omnipresent.

This word means 'Lord' and is used to refer to God in all His majesty and authority. In this verse, it highlights God's central role in the new Jerusalem, where He is the sovereign who reigns over all. This reinforces the idea that the relationship between God and humanity is direct, without intermediaries, which is a promise of intimacy and communion.

This term means 'lamb' and refers to Jesus Christ, often described as the Lamb of God in the New Testament. In this verse, it symbolizes sacrifice and redemption, emphasizing that Christ is at the heart of the new creation. It reminds believers that their access to God is based on the sacrifice of Jesus, who has opened the way to a direct relationship with the Father.

22.epoque: The book of Revelation was written at the end of the first century, in a context of persecution of Christians, which made their faith all the more precious and their hope for a glorious future essential.
22.passage: This passage is situated in the vision of the new Jerusalem, describing the eschatological reality where God dwells among His people. Chapter 21 presents the promise of complete restoration and perfect communion between God and humanity.
22.culture: In Jewish culture, the temple was the meeting place with God, symbolizing His presence among His people. The vision of a city without a temple challenges traditional conceptions of divinity and sacredness, heralding a new era of direct communion with God.
22.interpretation: The absence of a temple in the new Jerusalem indicates that God and the Lamb are present in an immediate and direct manner. This underscores that the relationship between God and His people is fully restored, without barriers or intermediaries, and that true worship is done in spirit and truth.
22.commentaire: This verse reminds us that our relationship with God does not depend on a physical place, but on our heart and our faith in Christ. In our daily lives, we are called to live in the awareness of God's presence, who dwells in us by His Spirit. Thus, every moment of our lives can become an act of worship, as we are the temple of the Holy Spirit.

mots.sens: This word means 'glory' and refers to splendor, majesty, and the recognition due to God. In the biblical context, God's glory is often associated with His manifest presence, power, and holiness. Here, it illuminates the heavenly city, emphasizing that divine light surpasses all created light, which has a profound theological significance regarding the nature of God as the source of all spiritual illumination.

The term 'lamb' refers to Jesus Christ, who is often designated as the Lamb of God in the New Testament. This word evokes the idea of sacrifice and redemption, as the lamb was a symbol of the offering for sin. In this verse, the Lamb is presented as the source of light, highlighting His central role in the plan of salvation and the revelation of God's glory.

23.epoque: The book of Revelation was written at the end of the first century, in a context of persecution of Christians under the Roman Empire, which influenced the author's visions of hope and God's final victory.
23.passage: This passage is situated in the description of the new Jerusalem, a symbol of the fullness of God's presence among His people. Chapter 21 evokes the final restoration and redemption, where God dwells with men in perfect communion.
23.culture: In Jewish culture, light is often associated with divine presence and revelation. The city without sun or moon represents a state of perfection where God's presence eliminates all forms of darkness or material need.
23.interpretation: This verse emphasizes that in the new Jerusalem, the glory of God and the Lamb are the ultimate source of light, symbolizing the perfect revelation of God. This indicates that in the coming kingdom, believers will live in direct and eternal communion with their Creator, without intermediaries.
23.commentaire: This passage reminds us that our hope does not rest on material elements, but on the presence of God Himself. As Christians, we are called to live in the light of His glory even now, witnessing the love and redemption of the Lamb. This encourages us to seek this light in our daily lives, reflecting God's glory to those around us.

mots.sens: This word means 'nation' or 'people', and it often designates a cultural or ethnic group. In the biblical context, it evokes the non-Jewish nations, highlighting the universality of the salvation offered by Christ. The theological significance here is that, in the kingdom of God, all nations gather and walk together in divine light, illustrating the inclusion of all in the plan of redemption.

This term translates to 'kings' and refers to rulers or authorities. In antiquity, kings were often seen as representatives of the power and glory of their nation. Spiritually, this underscores that even the most powerful on earth will recognize God's sovereignty and come to honor Him in His eternal kingdom.

This word means 'glory' and refers to splendor, majesty, and the recognition due to someone. In a biblical context, God's glory is often associated with His presence and power. In this verse, the glory that the kings bring to God emphasizes the acknowledgment of His supremacy and authority in the eternal kingdom.

This term means 'light' and often symbolizes truth, revelation, and life. In the Bible, light is associated with God's presence and spiritual guidance. In this verse, light represents the presence of Christ, who illuminates the nations and guides them toward truth and eternal life.

24.epoque: The book of Revelation was written at the end of the first century, in a context of persecution of Christians and the expectation of Christ's return. Believers faced major challenges, and this book offered them hope and encouragement.
24.passage: This verse is found in the context of the description of the new Jerusalem, a symbol of the kingdom of God. It highlights the transformation of creation and the final reconciliation of all things under Christ's reign.
24.culture: At that time, nations and kings had distinct roles in society, often in conflict. The fact that kings bring their glory to God shows a reversal of values where God's supremacy surpasses all human authority.
24.interpretation: Spiritually, this verse illustrates that all nations, without distinction, will walk in the light of Christ, who is the truth and the life. This underscores the universality of the Gospel message and the promise that all, including the powerful, will honor God in His kingdom.
24.commentaire: This passage reminds us that God's glory transcends all nations and human authorities. As believers, we are called to walk in this light and reflect the glory of Christ in our lives. This encourages us to live as citizens of the kingdom of God, witnessing His greatness and love in a world often shrouded in darkness.

mots.sens: The word 'πύλη' refers to a gate or entrance, often used in the context of cities or fortified places. In the New Testament, it symbolizes access to sacred spaces or communion with God. The theological significance here emphasizes that in the New Jerusalem, access to the divine presence is permanent and unobstructed.

The term 'νύξ' means night, often representing darkness, ignorance, or evil in the Bible. In this verse, the absence of night highlights the fullness of divine light and the revelation of God, symbolizing a state of perfection where there is no sin or suffering.

25.epoque: The book of Revelation was written at the end of the 1st century, in a context of persecution of Christians, which influenced the vision of a glorious future and renewed hope for believers.
25.passage: This verse is situated in the description of the New Jerusalem, a metaphor for the eternal dwelling of the redeemed, where the presence of God is fully manifest. Chapter 21 deals with the final restoration of all things and the promise of eternal communion with the Creator.
25.culture: In Jewish culture, light and darkness symbolize respectively the presence of God and the absence of His light. The vision of a city without night evokes a reality where God reigns without opposition, offering eternal security and peace.
25.interpretation: The absence of night and the permanence of open gates illustrate the security and accessibility of God's presence for His people. It also reflects the promise of eternal life where believers will never be separated from their Lord.
25.commentaire: This verse reminds us that in the New Jerusalem, communion with God is total and continuous. As believers, we can live in the assurance that our future is secured in Christ, where the light of His presence dispels all darkness. This encourages us to live in the light now, witnessing this hope in our daily lives.

mots.sens: This term means 'glory' and is often associated with the manifestation of divine majesty. In the biblical context, the glory of God is a reality that transcends humanity and evokes splendor, honor, and renown. Spiritually, this emphasizes that the glory of nations, while important, must be recognized as coming from God and for His glory.

This word means 'honor' and implies a recognition of the value or dignity of something or someone. In Scripture, honor is often linked to the acknowledgment of divine authority and the intrinsic worth of people created in the image of God. This reminds believers that honor should be given to God and to those who are faithful to Him.

This term translates to 'nations' and refers to groups of people often defined by cultural, linguistic, or ethnic characteristics. In the New Testament, it is often used to designate non-Jews, highlighting the universality of the Gospel message. Theologically, this emphasizes that all nations are called to worship God and bring their glory before Him.

26.epoque: The book of Revelation was written at the end of the 1st century, in a context of persecution of Christians and anticipation of the end times. Believers sought encouragement and promises from God in the face of trials.
26.passage: This verse is situated in the vision of the New Jerusalem, where God establishes His eternal kingdom. It highlights the beauty and richness of this new reality, where the nations bring their glory and honor before God.
26.culture: In antiquity, nations had their own gods and traditions, and glory was often associated with military power and wealth. This passage reverses that notion by placing the glory of nations in service to the supreme God.
26.interpretation: The contribution of the glory and honor of the nations in the New Jerusalem symbolizes the inclusion of all cultures in God's plan. It shows that, despite their differences, all nations are called to recognize God's sovereignty and offer their best in His honor.
26.commentaire: This verse reminds us that our service and efforts in this world should aim to glorify God. As believers, we are called to bring our own 'glory' and 'honor,' that is, our talents, resources, and worship, to contribute to the building of God's kingdom. This encourages us to see the value of our contribution, whatever it may be, in the grand divine plan.

mots.sens: This word means 'unclean,' 'impure,' and designates anything considered impure according to the Mosaic law. It evokes a spiritual and moral condition that excludes from the presence of God. In the context of this verse, it underscores the necessity of spiritual purification to enter the New Jerusalem.

This term translates to 'abomination' and refers to practices that provoke disgust and horror in the eyes of God. It encompasses idolatrous and immoral behaviors that are in direct opposition to divine holiness. Spiritually, this emphasizes the importance of living according to God's standards to be in communion with Him.

This word means 'name' or 'inscription' and is often used to designate a record. In the context of the book of life, it represents those who have been elected and saved by God's grace. This underscores the assurance that those whose names are written in this book have the promise of eternal life.

This term means 'lamb,' referring to Jesus Christ, the Lamb of God. It symbolizes the perfect sacrifice for sin and redemption. In this verse, the Lamb is central, as only those who are in relationship with Him, through faith, can hope to enter the New Jerusalem.

27.epoque: The book of Revelation was written at the end of the 1st century, in a context of persecution of Christians and anticipation of the end times.
27.passage: This passage is situated in the description of the New Jerusalem, a symbol of God's presence among His people, where holiness and purity are essential for entry.
27.culture: In Jewish culture, the idea of purity and impurity was central, and the Mosaic laws governed daily life. Abomination was synonymous with rejection by God.
27.interpretation: This verse underscores the necessity of spiritual purification to enter the presence of God. Only those who have been redeemed by the blood of the Lamb can hope to be admitted into the New Jerusalem.
27.commentaire: This passage reminds us of the importance of living a holy life in accordance with God's will. As Christians, we are called to distance ourselves from all that is impure and to anchor ourselves in our relationship with Christ, the Lamb. This encourages us to be vigilant in our spiritual walk, knowing that our name is written in the book of life.
